## Introduction

This case study is a version of the case study
[Uncertainty in Bayesian LOO-CV model comparison](https://users.aalto.fi/~ave/casestudies/LOO_uncertainty/loo_uncertainty.html).
It uses the same three examples and the same workflow. It replaces
`loo_compare()` with the `pred_measure()` family and `model_compare()`.

The `pred_measure()` family adds two choices to the workflow:

1. **The predictive measure.** The log score (`elpd`) is the default. Other
   scores answer other questions about the predictions.
2. **The predictive scheme.** PSIS-LOO is the default. Other schemes predict
   other kinds of new data.

This case study shows when these choices change the conclusion of a
comparison.

::: {.callout .callout-note}
**What this article does not cover**

+ **The arguments of the entry points.** See the
  [Predictive model performance: Predictive schemes with `pred_measure()`](pred-measure-workflow.html)
  article.
+ **The output columns of `model_compare()`.** See the
  [Model comparison: Explanation of `model_compare()`](model-comparison.html)
  article.
+ **Measure definitions.** See the
  [Predictive model performance: Overview of measures](overview-measures.html)
  article.
:::

### Uncertainty in the difference

`model_compare()` reports three quantities for `elpd`:

+ `elpd_diff`: the estimated difference in predictive performance.
+ `se_diff`: the standard error of that estimate.
+ `p_worse`: the probability that a model predicts worse than the reference
  model. This probability uses a normal approximation of the error of
  `elpd_diff`.

For the other measures, `model_compare()` reports `<measure>_diff` and
`<measure>_se_diff`.

### When the normal approximation is not reliable

Sivula et al. (2025) identify three scenarios in which `se_diff` and `p_worse`
can be miscalibrated:

| Scenario | Cause | Effect | Flag in `model_compare()` |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 1. Similar predictions | the models predict almost the same | `se_diff` underestimated, `p_worse` overestimated | `diag_diff`: `|elpd_diff| < 4` |
| 2. Misspecification with outliers | the model does not fit some observations | the estimator can be biased | none; use model checking |
| 3. Small data | few observations | `se_diff` too small | `diag_diff`: `N < 100` |

When both flags of `diag_diff` apply, `model_compare()` shows `N < 100` only.
For small data, a conservative heuristic is to double `se_diff`.

A second diagnostic, `diag_elpd`, flags models with high Pareto $\hat k$
values. Then the PSIS-LOO estimate itself can be biased. `diag_elpd` is
available for PSIS-LOO inputs only.

::: {.callout .callout-warning}
**The flags are for `elpd` only**

Sivula et al. (2025) studied the uncertainty of `elpd_diff`. Thus
`model_compare()` reports `p_worse` and `diag_diff` for `elpd` only. The other
measures can also have a miscalibrated `<measure>_se_diff` in the three
scenarios. Read their standard errors with the same caution.
:::

### Examples

| Example | $n$ | Scenarios | Score topic | Scheme topic |
| :--- | :---: | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| [Primate milk](#milk) | 17 | 1, 3 | log score and point error | PSIS-LOO |
| [Sleep study](#sleepstudy) | 144 | 2 | log score, `rps`, `srps` | PSIS-LOO, K-fold, grouped K-fold |
| [Roaches](#roaches) | 262 | 1, 2 | scores for counts | PSIS-LOO, K-fold |

In all examples, the true data-generating process is more complex than any of
the models. This is the usual applied setting.

```{r load-libraries, message=FALSE}
library(loo)
library(ggplot2)
theme_set(theme_minimal())

SEED <- 2030
CHAINS <- 2
ITER <- 400
```

Each fit uses `r CHAINS` chains with `r ITER / 2` draws after warmup, so
$S = `r CHAINS * ITER / 2`$. For $S = `r CHAINS * ITER / 2`$, the Pareto
$\hat k$ threshold is $\min(1 - 1/\log_{10} S,\, 0.7) =
`r round(min(1 - 1 / log10(CHAINS * ITER / 2), 0.7), 2)`$.

Two helper functions compute the measures of one fit under one scheme. They
use the entry points of the
[Predictive schemes](pred-measure-workflow.html) article:

```{r helpers}
loo_measure <- function(fit, measures) {
  loo_pred_measure(
    loo = brms::loo(fit, save_psis = TRUE),
    y = as.vector(brms::get_y(fit)),
    ypred = brms::posterior_predict(fit),
    mupred = brms::posterior_epred(fit),
    measures = measures
  )
}

kfold_measure <- function(fit, folds, measures) {
  kf <- brms::kfold(fit, folds = folds, save_fits = TRUE)
  kfold_pred_measure(
    y = as.vector(brms::get_y(fit)),
    ypred = brms::kfold_predict(kf, method = "predict")$yrep,
    mupred = brms::kfold_predict(kf, method = "fitted")$yrep,
    kfold = kf,
    measures = measures
  )
}
```

## Primate milk {#milk}

McElreath (2020) describes the primate milk data. A hypothesis states that
primates with larger brains produce more energetic milk. The data have 17
primate species. The outcome is the energy content of milk (`kcal.per.g`). The
predictors are the percent of the brain mass that is neocortex (`neocortex`)
and the logarithm of the female body mass (`log(mass)`).

```{r milk-data}
data(milk, package = "rethinking")
milk <- na.omit(milk)
milk$neocortex <- milk$neocortex.perc / 100
nrow(milk)
```

The four models are normal regressions with $\operatorname{normal}(0, 1)$
priors on the coefficients:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathrm{M}_1: &\quad \mathrm{kcal.per.g} \sim \operatorname{normal}(\alpha, \sigma) \\
\mathrm{M}_2: &\quad \mathrm{kcal.per.g} \sim \operatorname{normal}(\alpha + \beta_1\,\mathrm{neocortex}, \sigma) \\
\mathrm{M}_3: &\quad \mathrm{kcal.per.g} \sim \operatorname{normal}(\alpha + \beta_2\log(\mathrm{mass}), \sigma) \\
\mathrm{M}_4: &\quad \mathrm{kcal.per.g} \sim \operatorname{normal}(\alpha + \beta_1\,\mathrm{neocortex} + \beta_2\log(\mathrm{mass}), \sigma)
\end{aligned}
$$

```{r milk-fit, results="hide", message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
milk_1 <- brms::brm(kcal.per.g ~ 1, data = milk,
                    chains = CHAINS, iter = ITER, seed = SEED, refresh = 0)
milk_2 <- update(milk_1, formula. = ~ neocortex, newdata = milk,
                 prior = brms::prior(normal(0, 1), class = "b"),
                 seed = SEED, refresh = 0)
milk_3 <- update(milk_1, formula. = ~ log(mass), newdata = milk,
                 prior = brms::prior(normal(0, 1), class = "b"),
                 seed = SEED, refresh = 0)
milk_4 <- update(milk_1, formula. = ~ neocortex + log(mass), newdata = milk,
                 prior = brms::prior(normal(0, 1), class = "b"),
                 seed = SEED, refresh = 0)
```

**Model checking.** Before the comparison, check the calibration of the
predictive distributions with LOO-PIT (Tesso and Vehtari, 2026). The
LOO-PIT values of a calibrated model are close to uniform:

```{r milk-pit, fig.height=3}
brms::pp_check(milk_4, type = "loo_pit_ecdf")
```

<!-- TODO: check the LOO-PIT plots of milk_1 to milk_3 after the render -->

**Measures.** The comparison uses four measures:

+ `elpd`: the log score of the whole predictive distribution.
+ `rps`: the continuous ranked probability score, in the units of the outcome.
+ `rmse`: the error of the point prediction.
+ `r2`: the predictive $R^2$, the share of the variance that the model
  explains.

```{r milk-measures, warning=FALSE}
measures_milk <- c("elpd", "rps", "rmse", "r2")

set.seed(SEED)
comp_milk <- model_compare(list(
  M_1 = loo_measure(milk_1, measures_milk),
  M_2 = loo_measure(milk_2, measures_milk),
  M_3 = loo_measure(milk_3, measures_milk),
  M_4 = loo_measure(milk_4, measures_milk)
))
comp_milk
```

**Result.** The data have 17 observations. Thus `diag_diff` shows `N < 100`
for all comparisons (Scenario 3). The differences are also small
(Scenario 1). The flag `|elpd_diff| < 4` is not shown, because `N < 100`
has priority.

**Doubled standard error.** A conservative heuristic doubles `se_diff`. This
does not correct the skewness of the error distribution. It shows how
sensitive `p_worse` is:

```{r milk-double-se}
data.frame(
  model = comp_milk$model,
  p_worse = round(comp_milk$p_worse, 2),
  p_worse_2se = round(
    stats::pnorm(0, comp_milk$elpd_diff, 2 * comp_milk$se_diff), 2
  )
)
```

**Other measures.** Do the other measures rank the models in the same order?

```{r milk-all}
print(comp_milk, measures = "all")
```

<!-- TODO: check after the render that the ranking agrees across measures -->

`print()` names one reference model for each measure. The reference model is
the best model on that measure. Thus the reference can differ between
measures. `rmse` and `r2` score only the predictive mean, `mupred`. They
ignore the predictive uncertainty. `elpd` and `rps` score the whole predictive
distribution.

**Interpretation.** With 17 observations, the uncertainty in all differences is
large. No measure can separate the models reliably. Collect more data if
possible. The predictive distribution includes the noise of the data model.
Thus a comparison of predictive performance often has more uncertainty than
the posterior of the parameters (Wang and Gelman, 2015). For a small model, also
look at the posterior of the quantities of interest:

```{r milk-posterior}
brms::fixef(milk_4)
```

`neocortex` and `log(mass)` are collinear. In $\mathrm{M}_4$, the two
coefficients together carry the information. Each covariate alone carries
little information. This explains why $\mathrm{M}_2$ and $\mathrm{M}_3$
predict no better than the intercept-only model $\mathrm{M}_1$.

## Sleep study {#sleepstudy}

Belenky et al. (2003) studied chronic sleep restriction. The `sleepstudy` data
(**lme4**) hold the average reaction time (ms) of 18 subjects. The subjects
slept at most three hours each night. Days 0 and 1 were adaptation and
training, so the case study keeps days 2 to 9. This gives 144 observations.

```{r sleep-data}
data("sleepstudy", package = "lme4")
sleepstudy2 <- subset(sleepstudy, Days >= 2)
nrow(sleepstudy2)
```

The three models use a normal data model and the default priors of **brms**:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathrm{M}_1: &\quad \mathrm{Reaction} \sim \mathrm{Days} \\
\mathrm{M}_2: &\quad \mathrm{Reaction} \sim \mathrm{Days} + (1 \mid \mathrm{Subject}) \\
\mathrm{M}_3: &\quad \mathrm{Reaction} \sim \mathrm{Days} + (\mathrm{Days} \mid \mathrm{Subject})
\end{aligned}
$$

The design of the study suggests $\mathrm{M}_3$. The comparison shows how much
information the data have about the varying intercepts and slopes.

```{r sleep-fit, results="hide", message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
sleep_1 <- brms::brm(Reaction ~ Days, data = sleepstudy2,
                     family = gaussian(),
                     chains = CHAINS, iter = ITER, seed = SEED, refresh = 0)
sleep_2 <- update(sleep_1, formula. = ~ . + (1 | Subject),
                  seed = SEED, refresh = 0)
sleep_3 <- update(sleep_1, formula. = ~ . + (Days | Subject),
                  seed = SEED, refresh = 0)
```

### PSIS-LOO and the log score

First, compare the models on `elpd` with PSIS-LOO:

```{r sleep-loo, warning=FALSE}
loo_sleep <- lapply(
  list(M_1 = sleep_1, M_2 = sleep_2, M_3 = sleep_3),
  brms::loo, save_psis = TRUE
)
model_compare(lapply(loo_sleep, function(x) loo_pred_measure(loo = x)))
```

`print()` reports the models with high Pareto $\hat k$ values, and
`diag_elpd` flags them. A high $\hat k$ can come from misspecification or from
a flexible model. Then the PSIS-LOO estimate can be optimistic.

**Reloo.** `reloo = TRUE` refits the model once for each observation with a
high $\hat k$. This makes `elpd_loo` accurate.

```{r sleep-reloo, results="hide", message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
reloo_sleep <- lapply(
  list(M_1 = sleep_1, M_2 = sleep_2, M_3 = sleep_3),
  brms::loo, reloo = TRUE, save_psis = TRUE
)
```

```{r sleep-reloo-compare}
model_compare(lapply(reloo_sleep, function(x) loo_pred_measure(loo = x)))
```

::: {.callout .callout-warning}
**Reloo gives a correct `elpd` only**

`reloo` replaces `elpd_loo` of the refitted observations. It keeps the old
PSIS weights for the other measures. Thus request only `elpd`, `mlpd`, or `ic`
from a `loo` object after `reloo`. For the other measures, use K-fold
([see below](#sleep-scores)). The
[Predictive schemes](pred-measure-workflow.html#computing-loo) article has the
details.
:::

### Model checking

A more accurate `elpd` does not fix a misspecified model. Outliers can still
make the normal approximation of the uncertainty inaccurate (Scenario 2).
Check the calibration with LOO-PIT:

```{r sleep-pit, fig.height=3, warning=FALSE}
brms::pp_check(sleep_3, type = "loo_pit_ecdf")
```

<!-- TODO: check after the render that the curve of M_3 is S-shaped -->

An S-shaped LOO-PIT ECDF shows predictive distributions that are too wide. The
LOO intervals show the cause:

```{r sleep-intervals, warning=FALSE}
brms::pp_check(sleep_3, type = "loo_intervals")
```

A few observations lie far outside their predictive intervals. These outliers
increase the residual scale $\sigma$ of the normal model. Thus the predictive
distributions are too wide for the other observations.

**Pointwise differences.** The pointwise `elpd` differences of
$\mathrm{M}_3$ and $\mathrm{M}_2$ show the effect of the outliers:

```{r sleep-pointwise}
pointwise_diff <- function(loo_a, loo_b) {
  loo_a$pointwise[, "elpd_loo"] - loo_b$pointwise[, "elpd_loo"]
}

ggplot(data.frame(i = seq_len(nrow(sleepstudy2)),
                  diff = pointwise_diff(reloo_sleep$M_3, reloo_sleep$M_2)),
       aes(i, diff)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_point() +
  labs(x = "observation", y = "pointwise elpd difference (M_3 - M_2)")
```

$\mathrm{M}_3$ is better for most observations. A few observations have a
large difference. These large values make the normal approximation of
`elpd_diff` less accurate.

### Student-t models

A Student-$t$ data model has heavier tails. It can accommodate the outliers
without an increase of the scale for all observations. Models
$\mathrm{M}_{1t}$, $\mathrm{M}_{2t}$, and $\mathrm{M}_{3t}$ use the formulas of
$\mathrm{M}_1$ to $\mathrm{M}_3$ with `family = student()`:

```{r sleep-fit-t, results="hide", message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
sleep_1t <- update(sleep_1, family = brms::student(), seed = SEED, refresh = 0)
sleep_2t <- update(sleep_2, family = brms::student(), seed = SEED, refresh = 0)
sleep_3t <- update(sleep_3, family = brms::student(), seed = SEED, refresh = 0)

reloo_sleep_t <- lapply(
  list(M_1t = sleep_1t, M_2t = sleep_2t, M_3t = sleep_3t),
  brms::loo, reloo = TRUE, save_psis = TRUE
)
```

```{r sleep-pit-t, fig.height=3, warning=FALSE}
brms::pp_check(sleep_3t, type = "loo_pit_ecdf")
```

Compare $\mathrm{M}_3$ and $\mathrm{M}_{3t}$:

```{r sleep-compare-3t}
model_compare(list(
  M_3 = loo_pred_measure(loo = reloo_sleep$M_3),
  M_3t = loo_pred_measure(loo = reloo_sleep_t$M_3t)
))
```

$\mathrm{M}_3$ is misspecified, so its `se_diff` can be inflated. Thus the
true probability that $\mathrm{M}_{3t}$ predicts better is likely even higher
than `1 - p_worse`.

Compare the three Student-$t$ models:

```{r sleep-compare-t}
comp_sleep_t <- model_compare(
  lapply(reloo_sleep_t, function(x) loo_pred_measure(loo = x))
)
comp_sleep_t
```

The models pass the model checking. $n = 144$ is larger than 100. If the
differences are not small, the normal approximation is likely well calibrated.

```{r sleep-pointwise-t}
ggplot(data.frame(i = seq_len(nrow(sleepstudy2)),
                  diff = pointwise_diff(reloo_sleep_t$M_3t,
                                        reloo_sleep_t$M_2t)),
       aes(i, diff)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_point() +
  labs(x = "observation", y = "pointwise elpd difference (M_3t - M_2t)")
```

<!-- TODO: check after the render that the t-model plot has no large outliers -->

### Choice of the score {#sleep-scores}

The log score is a strictly proper and local score: it uses only the predictive
density at the observed value (Gneiting and Raftery, 2007). This makes it
sensitive to observations in the tails. A single outlier can dominate
`elpd_diff`. Two other proper scores react differently to outliers:

| Score | Uses | Penalty for an outlier | Use when |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| `elpd` | density at $y_i$ | grows with $-\log p(y_i)$, unbounded | the whole predictive distribution matters, including the tails |
| `rps` | distance between $y_i$ and the predictive draws | grows linearly with the distance | the distance to the observation matters; the units of $y$ help communication |
| `srps` | `rps`, scaled by the predictive spread | grows with the distance relative to the spread | the predictive spread differs strongly between observations |

`srps` is the scaled CRPS of Bolin and Wallin (2023). It is locally scale
invariant: observations with a wide predictive distribution do not dominate the
average. `rps` does not have this property.

**K-fold.** `rps` and `srps` need reliable weights for each observation. The
models have high Pareto $\hat k$ values, and `reloo` corrects `elpd` only.
Thus compute all measures with 10-fold cross-validation. All models use the
same folds, so the pointwise differences are paired:

```{r sleep-kfold, results="hide", message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
measures_sleep <- c("elpd", "rps", "srps", "rmse")

set.seed(SEED)
folds_sleep <- kfold_split_random(K = 10, N = nrow(sleepstudy2))

kfold_sleep <- lapply(
  list(M_1 = sleep_1, M_2 = sleep_2, M_3 = sleep_3,
       M_1t = sleep_1t, M_2t = sleep_2t, M_3t = sleep_3t),
  kfold_measure, folds = folds_sleep, measures = measures_sleep
)
```

**Normal versus Student-$t$.** Compare $\mathrm{M}_3$ and $\mathrm{M}_{3t}$ on
all measures:

```{r sleep-kfold-3t}
comp_sleep_3t <- model_compare(kfold_sleep[c("M_3", "M_3t")])
print(comp_sleep_3t, measures = "all")
```

<!-- TODO: check after the render that the text below matches the output -->

The scores weigh the outliers differently. `elpd` gives a large penalty to an
observation in the far tail of the normal model. `rps` grows only linearly
with the distance, so it shows a smaller advantage for $\mathrm{M}_{3t}$.
`rmse` scores the predictive mean only. The two models have similar means, so
`rmse` cannot see the difference in the tails.

**All six models.** Compare all models on `srps`:

```{r sleep-kfold-all}
comp_sleep_kfold <- model_compare(kfold_sleep)
print(comp_sleep_kfold, measures = c("elpd", "srps"))
```

A conclusion that holds for several proper scores is more robust than a
conclusion from one score. If the scores disagree, the models differ in the
part of the predictive distribution that one score emphasizes.

### Choice of the predictive scheme {#sleep-schemes}

LOO and random K-fold leave out single observations. The other observations of
the same subject stay in the training data. Thus these schemes answer this
question: how well does the model predict a new day of a *known* subject?

A different question is: how well does the model predict a *new* subject?
Then leave out all observations of a subject together. This is leave-one-group-out
or grouped K-fold cross-validation. Random cross-validation of grouped data
answers the second question too optimistically (Roberts et al., 2017).

`kfold_split_grouped()` puts the observations of each subject in one fold.
With 18 subjects and $K = 6$, each fold holds three subjects:

```{r sleep-grouped, results="hide", message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
set.seed(SEED)
folds_subject <- kfold_split_grouped(K = 6, x = sleepstudy2$Subject)

grouped_sleep <- lapply(
  list(M_1t = sleep_1t, M_2t = sleep_2t, M_3t = sleep_3t),
  kfold_measure, folds = folds_subject, measures = measures_sleep
)
```

For a held-out subject, `brms::kfold_predict()` draws new varying effects from
the population distribution (`allow_new_levels = TRUE`).

```{r sleep-grouped-compare}
comp_sleep_grouped <- model_compare(grouped_sleep)
print(comp_sleep_grouped, measures = c("elpd", "srps"))
```

Compare the result with random 10-fold for the same models:

```{r sleep-random-compare}
print(model_compare(kfold_sleep[c("M_1t", "M_2t", "M_3t")]),
      measures = c("elpd", "srps"))
```

<!-- TODO: check after the render that the text below matches the output -->

For a new subject, the varying effects carry no information about that
subject. The models can only use the population distribution of the effects.
Thus the differences between the models are smaller than with random folds.
The remaining difference shows how well each model describes the variation
between subjects.

**Interpretation.** The effect of sleep restriction is large. The main
conclusion is the same for all models. $\mathrm{M}_{3t}$ passes the model
checking and predicts best. Continue the analysis with the posterior of
$\mathrm{M}_{3t}$. Choose the scheme from the intended use of the model: new
days of the same subjects, or new subjects.

## Roaches {#roaches}

Gelman and Hill (2007, Sec. 8.3) describe the roaches data. A pest management
treatment was applied to 160 apartments, and 104 apartments were controls. The
outcome `y` is the number of roaches caught in traps. The traps were used for
different numbers of days. The predictors are:

+ `sqrt_roach1`: the square root of the pre-treatment roach count.
+ `treatment`: an indicator of the treatment.
+ `senior`: an indicator of a building for elderly residents.
+ `offset(log(exposure2))`: the logarithm of the number of trap days.

```{r roaches-data}
data(roaches, package = "rstanarm")
roaches$sqrt_roach1 <- sqrt(roaches$roach1)
nrow(roaches)
```

The models use the same linear predictor with different data models. The
coefficients have $\operatorname{normal}(0, 1)$ priors. The negative-binomial
shape has an $\operatorname{inv\text{-}gamma}(0.4, 0.3)$ prior.

| Model | Data model | Linear predictor |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| $\mathrm{M}_1$ | Poisson | linear in `sqrt_roach1` |
| $\mathrm{M}_2$ | negative-binomial | linear in `sqrt_roach1` |
| $\mathrm{M}_3$ | zero-inflated negative-binomial | linear in `sqrt_roach1` |
| $\mathrm{M}_4$ | zero-inflated negative-binomial | spline of `sqrt_roach1` |

The zero-inflation part of $\mathrm{M}_3$ and $\mathrm{M}_4$ uses the same
predictors, with its own coefficients.

```{r roaches-fit, results="hide", message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
f_roach <- y ~ sqrt_roach1 + treatment + senior + offset(log(exposure2))
f_zi <- zi ~ sqrt_roach1 + treatment + senior + offset(log(exposure2))
prior_b <- brms::prior(normal(0, 1), class = "b")
prior_shape <- brms::prior(inv_gamma(0.4, 0.3), class = "shape")
prior_zi <- brms::prior(normal(0, 1), class = "b", dpar = "zi") +
  brms::prior(normal(0, 1), class = "Intercept", dpar = "zi")

roach_1 <- brms::brm(f_roach, data = roaches, family = poisson(),
                     prior = prior_b,
                     chains = CHAINS, iter = ITER, seed = SEED, refresh = 0)
roach_2 <- brms::brm(f_roach, data = roaches, family = brms::negbinomial(),
                     prior = prior_b + prior_shape,
                     chains = CHAINS, iter = ITER, seed = SEED, refresh = 0)
roach_3 <- brms::brm(brms::bf(f_roach, f_zi), data = roaches,
                     family = brms::zero_inflated_negbinomial(),
                     prior = prior_b + prior_shape + prior_zi,
                     chains = CHAINS, iter = ITER, seed = SEED, refresh = 0)
roach_4 <- brms::brm(
  brms::bf(y ~ s(sqrt_roach1) + treatment + senior + offset(log(exposure2)),
           zi ~ s(sqrt_roach1) + treatment + senior + offset(log(exposure2))),
  data = roaches, family = brms::zero_inflated_negbinomial(),
  prior = prior_b + prior_shape + prior_zi,
  chains = CHAINS, iter = ITER, seed = SEED, refresh = 0
)
```

### PSIS-LOO and the log score

```{r roaches-loo, warning=FALSE}
loo_roach <- lapply(
  list(M_1 = roach_1, M_2 = roach_2, M_3 = roach_3),
  brms::loo, save_psis = TRUE
)
model_compare(lapply(loo_roach, function(x) loo_pred_measure(loo = x)))
```

The Poisson model $\mathrm{M}_1$ has many high Pareto $\hat k$ values. It is
underdispersed for these data (Scenario 2). See the
[roaches case study](https://users.aalto.fi/~ave/modelselection/roaches.html)
for the model checking. The difference to $\mathrm{M}_1$ is so large that the
bias of PSIS-LOO does not change the conclusion.

### Scores for count data

For counts, the predictive distribution is discrete. These scores are useful
(Czado et al., 2009):

| Score | For counts |
| :--- | :--- |
| `elpd` | the log of the predictive probability of the observed count |
| `rps` | the ranked probability score; it rewards probability on counts near the observed count |
| `mae` | the absolute error of the predictive mean |
| `rmse` | the squared error of the predictive mean; large counts dominate it |

The counts range from 0 to `r max(roaches$y)`. Thus `rmse` depends mostly on
the few apartments with many roaches. `mae` and `rps` are less sensitive to
them.

**K-fold.** The Poisson model has many high $\hat k$ values, and
`reloo` would refit it many times. `rps`, `mae`, and `rmse` also need reliable
weights. Thus compute all measures with 10-fold cross-validation:

```{r roaches-kfold, results="hide", message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
measures_roach <- c("elpd", "rps", "mae", "rmse")

set.seed(SEED)
folds_roach <- kfold_split_random(K = 10, N = nrow(roaches))

kfold_roach <- lapply(
  list(M_1 = roach_1, M_2 = roach_2, M_3 = roach_3, M_4 = roach_4),
  kfold_measure, folds = folds_roach, measures = measures_roach
)
```

```{r roaches-kfold-compare}
comp_roach <- model_compare(kfold_roach[c("M_1", "M_2", "M_3")])
print(comp_roach, measures = "all")
```

<!-- TODO: check after the render that the text below matches the output -->

The zero-inflated negative-binomial model $\mathrm{M}_3$ is best on `elpd`.
The data have more than 100 observations, and the difference to $\mathrm{M}_2$
is not small. Thus the normal approximation is likely well calibrated.

`mae` and `rmse` score the predictive mean only. A Poisson and a
negative-binomial model with the same mean get the same point error. Thus
these measures cannot detect the overdispersion that `elpd` and `rps` detect.

### A small difference

$\mathrm{M}_3$ uses an ad hoc square root of the pre-treatment count.
$\mathrm{M}_4$ replaces the linear term with a spline:

```{r roaches-spline}
comp_roach_spline <- model_compare(kfold_roach[c("M_3", "M_4")])
print(comp_roach_spline, measures = "all")
```

<!-- TODO: check after the render that diag_diff shows |elpd_diff| < 4 -->

Here $n > 100$, so `diag_diff` can show the flag `|elpd_diff| < 4`
(Scenario 1). In the milk example, the difference was also small, but
`N < 100` had priority. When the difference is this small, the models predict
almost equally well. Use either model.

## Summary

### Which score?

| Question | Score | Notes |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| How good is the whole predictive distribution? | `elpd` | default; strictly proper; sensitive to outliers; `p_worse` and `diag_diff` are available |
| How close is the predictive distribution to the observation? | `rps` | proper; in the units of $y$; good for counts and ordered outcomes |
| Does the comparison depend on observations with a wide predictive spread? | `srps` | proper; locally scale invariant |
| How good is the point prediction? | `mae`, `rmse` | ignore the predictive uncertainty; easy to communicate |
| Which share of the variance does the model explain? | `r2` | relative to the variance of $y$; easy to communicate |

Choose the score from the use of the predictions before the comparison.
Report several scores when they answer different questions.

### Which scheme?

| Question | Scheme | Entry point |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| A new observation, exchangeable with the data | PSIS-LOO | `loo_pred_measure()` |
| As above, with many high Pareto $\hat k$ | K-fold, random folds | `kfold_pred_measure()` |
| A new group, for example a new subject | K-fold, grouped folds | `kfold_pred_measure()` with `kfold_split_grouped()` |
| Data withheld from the start | test data | `test_pred_measure()` |
| The future of a time series | leave-future-out | not in the `pred_measure()` family; see the [LFO vignette](../loo2-lfo.html) |

### Which uncertainty check?

1. Check the models before the comparison, for example with LOO-PIT.
2. Read `diag_elpd`. If it flags a model, use `reloo` or moment matching for
   `elpd`, or K-fold for all measures.
3. Read `diag_diff`. With `N < 100`, double `se_diff` as a sensitivity check.
   With `|elpd_diff| < 4`, the models predict almost equally well.
4. Plot the pointwise differences. A few large values show outliers.
